en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Refutation of Objections.
8. The Question of the Footprint Mark “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘When the Blessed One walks, this insentient great earth sinks where it is high and rises where it is low. Yet, on the other hand, you say:”
“The Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter.
But as for that splinter which fell upon the Blessed One’s foot, why did that splinter not turn back from the Blessed One’s foot?

If, venerable Nāgasena, when the Blessed One walks this insentient great earth rises where it is low and sinks where it is high, then the statement that “the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter” is false.
“If the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter, then indeed the statement that ‘as the Blessed One walks, this insentient great earth sinks where it is low and rises where it is high’ is false.
This too is a dilemma from both sides that has come upon you; it must be resolved by you.
“It is true, Great King, that as the Blessed One walks, this insentient great earth—”

What was high sank down, and what was low rose up; moreover, the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter, yet that splinter did not fall there of its own nature, but fell through the deliberate effort of Devadatta.

For many hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, Great King, Devadatta harbored malice toward the Blessed One; because of that malice, he released [the rock], thinking, “I shall hurl a stone as large as a gabled house upon the Blessed One.”

“Then two rocks rose up from the earth and caught that stone; then, by the collision of those two, a splinter broke off from the rock and, falling hither and thither, fell at the feet of the Blessed One.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, just as the two rocks caught the stone, so too must the splinter have been caught?
“Even though it was caught, Your Majesty, some of it here trickled away and flowed out; it did not remain in place.”
Just as, Great King, water taken in the hand trickles and flows out through the gaps between the fingers and does not remain in place;
and just as milk, buttermilk, honey, ghee, oil, fish broth, or meat broth taken in the hand trickles and flows out through the gaps between the fingers and does not remain in place;
In the same way, Great King, when two rocks met for the purpose of colliding, a splinter broke off from the stone and, falling hither or thither, fell at the Blessed One’s feet.

Or again, Great King, just as sand as fine, subtle, and minute as dust, when grasped in a fist, trickles and flows through the spaces between the fingers and does not remain in place; so it was with that splinter.
In the same way, Great King, when two rocks met for the purpose of colliding, a splinter broke off from the stone and, falling hither or thither, landed at the Blessed One’s feet.

Or again, Great King, just as a morsel taken into the mouth might escape from someone’s mouth and fall away or drop out, not remaining in its place; so too did that splinter fall at the Blessed One’s feet.
“In the same way, Great King, when two rocks met for the purpose of colliding, a splinter broke off from the stone and, falling hither or thither, fell at the feet of the Blessed One.
“Let it be so, Bhante Nāgasena; the rock was received by the rocks. But should honor also be paid to the splinter, just as it is to the great earth?
“Great King, there are these twelve who do not pay honor.”
Which twelve? One who is lustful does not show respect because of lust; one who is hateful because of hatred; one who is deluded because of delusion;
one who is arrogant because of conceit; one who lacks virtue because of a lack of distinction; one who is overly rigid because of a lack of restraint; and one who is base because of a base nature.
One who obeys out of lack of independence; one who is wicked out of stinginess; one who causes suffering because he has been made to suffer in return;
one who is greedy because he is overcome by craving; and one who is driven on because he seeks to achieve his own ends—these do not show respect.
These, O Great King, are the twelve who do not show respect.
And that splinter, having broken off due to the impact with the stone, fell at the feet of the Blessed One, falling in no particular direction or place.
Just as, Great King, fine, subtle, minute dust, driven by the force of the wind, scatters in no particular direction or place;
even so, Great King, that splinter, having broken off due to the impact with the stone, fell at the feet of the Blessed One, falling in no particular direction or place.
"But if, Great King, that flake were not separate from the rock, those other rocks would have caught it as it flew up.

However, Great King, this flake was neither on the ground nor in the air; having broken off by the force of the impact against the rock, it fell in no particular direction, falling here or there, and landed at the Blessed One’s feet.
Or just as, Great King, an old leaf blown up by a whirlwind falls in no particular direction, falling here or there."
“In the same way, Great King, this splinter, falling in no particular direction due to the force of the blow from the rock, fell at the Blessed One’s foot.
Moreover, Great King, it was for the sake of the experience of suffering by Devadatta—the ungrateful and stingy one—that the splinter fell at the Blessed One’s foot.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The eighth question: The Foot-Stone.
